<reason>B won the central theoretical clash. A defined the motion as a foreseeability-plus-reasonableness test, which is functionally negligence — and never explained what product-liability-style responsibility adds over the negligence, consumer-protection, and sector law B showed already owns A's parade case. B's strategic concession (deny the mechanism, not the responsibility) forced A to defend the motion's distinctive work in the hard space, where A's own answers to pressure questions sprang two traps: foreseeability defined by the provider's own evals taxes diligent red-teaming and immunizes those who don't look, and reasonableness frozen to contemporaneous industry practice punishes only laggards, leaving every first victim uncompensated. Neither point was answered in A's closing, and B flagged the omission. A landed real doctrinal hits (no complete spec is required in design-defect law; the contemporaneous snapshot blunts the retroactivity charge) and bounded "ordinary use" via marketed purposes, but the closing gambit — "CON admits the decisive case" — collapsed into B's duplication argument, and open-source/publication-as-liability-event went unrebutted. B's clipped Rebuttal 1 is a modest execution cost (reflected in reb_b), but the lost text was a summary tail whose substance re-landed later. B built the cleaner, better-defended path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.4–B4.6: B turned A's own pressure-question answers against the motion — foreseeability via the provider's own evals creates a perverse "tax on transparency," and the snapshot standard only ever punishes laggards — a fork A never addressed in its closing, letting B crystallize: the rule duplicates negligence where cases are easy and misfires where they are hard.</best_rebuttal>
